blocks.text: **The problem.** You're given an array `asteroids` of non-zero integers in a row. The absolute value is an asteroid's **size**; the sign is its **direction** — positive moves **right**, negative moves **left**. All move at the same speed. When two meet, the **smaller one explodes**; if they're the same size, **both** explode. Asteroids moving the same way never meet. Return the asteroids left after all collisions.

blocks.alt: Asteroids 5 moving right, 10 moving right and 5 moving left. The left-mover 5 meets the right-mover 10; 10 is bigger, so the 5 explodes. Result: 5 and 10.

blocks.code:
Input: [5, 10, -5]     Output: [5, 10]     -5 hits 10 and explodes
Input: [8, -8]         Output: []          same size: both explode
Input: [10, 2, -5]     Output: [10]        -5 destroys 2, then hits 10 and explodes
Input: [-2, -1, 1, 2]  Output: [-2, -1, 1, 2]   left-movers on the left never meet right-movers

blocks.text: A collision needs a right-mover **followed by** a left-mover. And when a left-mover destroys an asteroid, it keeps going and meets the **next survivor to its left** — the newest item reacting with the latest survivor, then the one before that. That's the stack signal.
1. Brute force: resolve the first collision, then start over
Scan for the first adjacent pair where a right-mover is followed by a left-mover. Resolve it, remove the loser(s), and rescan from the beginning. Stop when a full scan finds no such pair.
**Time O(n²), space O(n).** Each collision removes at least one asteroid, but every rescan and every removal from the middle of the array costs O(n).

Process asteroids left to right, keeping the **survivors so far** on a stack. A new asteroid can only collide if it moves **left** and the top survivor moves **right**. While that's true, fight: if the top is smaller, it explodes (pop) and the newcomer fights the next survivor; if they're equal, both go; if the top is bigger, the newcomer explodes. A newcomer that survives is pushed.

blocks.alt: Processing 10, 2, -5. The stack holds 10 and 2, both moving right. -5 arrives: it beats 2 (pop), then meets 10 and explodes. The stack ends as [10].

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n).** Every asteroid is pushed at most once and popped at most once. The stack holds the answer in order, bottom to top.
3. Best solution: use the input array as the stack

The survivors are always a **prefix** of what we've read, so they can live in the **front of the input array itself**. Keep an index `top`: `asteroids[0..top]` are the survivors. Pushing writes into `asteroids[top + 1]` — a slot we've already read, so nothing is lost. No second array at all.

blocks.alt: The input array doubles as the stack. Slots 0 to top hold the survivors; slots between top and the current asteroid were already read and can be overwritten; the rest have not been read yet.

blocks.caption: The green prefix is the survivors stack; it lives inside the input array.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1) extra** — the input array is reused as the stack. Writing into `asteroids[top + 1]` is safe because `top + 1` is never past the asteroid currently being read. (If the caller needs the original array afterwards, copy it first — or use the optimal solution.)

blocks.alt: Brute force: O(n²) time, O(n) space. Optimal: O(n) time, O(n) space. Best: O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

items: **No collisions** — `[-2, -1, 1, 2]`: left-movers on the left, right-movers on the right.
**Equal sizes** — `[8, -8]`: both explode, the answer is empty.
**One big left-mover** — `[1, 2, 3, -10]`: it destroys everything and survives.
**A chain that stops** — `[10, 2, -5]`: -5 destroys 2, then loses to 10.
**Several left-movers in a row** — `[1, -2, -2, -2]`: the first -2 destroys 1, the rest fly away.
